1.pericope_label: And the word of the Lord came unto Jonah the second time, saying, Arise, go unto Nineveh, that great city, and preach unto it the preaching that I bid thee.

schools.summary: Reads the renewed charge forward, as a command to proclaim what God would yet say, and takes the city's greatness as reckoned in God's own estimation, pointing toward the motive for sparing it.
Treat the second commission as legally necessary and as pure grace: no prophet may act on a lapsed warrant, and the restored office was earned by no merit whatever.
Identifies the charge with the oracle already given, and dwells on the herald's earnestness while distinguishing it sharply from mere noise.
Makes the renewal at once a pardon and a probation, and finds in God's continued use of a man the best evidence of his being at peace with him.

debates.question: Does the preaching he is bidden to cry mean the message already given or one still to come?

positions.position: The same oracle as before, which he was now prepared to obey.
A message still to be delivered: he is to proclaim what God would say to him.

outliers.claim: Treats the renewal as a legal necessity rather than a kindness, since acting on a lapsed commission is dangerous, and cites the Israelites cut down by the Amalekites for going up without the word of the Lord.
Sees the whole point in the gratuity of the restoration: a man who had by flight deprived himself of every favour recovers office and honour by no merit at all.

themes: And the word of the Lord came unto Jonah the second time, saying,
Arise, go unto Nineveh, that great city, and preach unto it the preaching that I bid thee.

3.pericope_label: So Jonah arose, and went unto Nineveh, according to the word of the Lord. Now Nineveh was an exceeding great city of three days’ journey. And Jonah began to enter into the city a day’s journey, and he cried, and said, Yet forty days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown.

schools.summary: Weighs the tense, the idiom that calls the place a city great to God, and the measure of the three days, while dismissing as trivial the questions the writer never meant to answer.
Read the prompt obedience as the fruit of chastisement and as the energy of faith in a man obscure, alone and unarmed but sent from above.
Supplies the geographers' figures for the circuit and defends the Hebrew number against the ancient versions on grounds of both text and sense.

debates.question: What was the prophet doing during the day's journey?

positions.position: Walking the circuit of the walls, three days round, and announcing the message from them.
Entering the streets and beginning to preach at once, so that before one day was out the whole city was alarmed.
The question is trivial, since the writer supplies no data for dimensions but only a general sense of vast size.

outliers.claim: Notes that the past tense seems to imply the city no longer existed when the account was written, while warning that a Hebrew tense cannot be judged by the analogy of modern languages.
Traces the ancient versions' three days to a copyist's confusion of Greek numerals, and argues that forty days were needed to leave room for reflection, where three would have produced only terror.

themes: So Jonah arose, and went unto Nineveh, according to the word of the Lord. Now Nineveh was an exceeding great city of three days’ journey.
And Jonah began to enter into the city a day’s journey, and he cried, and said, Yet forty days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown.

5.pericope_label: So the people of Nineveh believed God, and proclaimed a fast, and put on sackcloth, from the greatest of them even to the least of them.

schools.summary: Renders the phrase believed in God, hears an implied reproach of those slow to credit warnings sent to themselves, and takes the fast as the people's own spontaneous act.
Locate the faith in a word heard as God's rather than man's, and infer from it that the sermon must have convicted of guilt as well as threatened ruin.
Holds the threatening conditional though the condition was unexpressed, and marks the fast as unequalled in extent, depth and effect.
Sets this repentance against Israel's obstinacy under far greater advantages, and itemises the articles the Ninevites came to believe.

debates.question: Did a report of the prophet's own deliverance help produce their faith?

positions.position: No: their faith was the effect of divine power accompanying the preaching, not the persuasion of men.
Some think so, but of this we have no certainty.
Their faith rested on the preacher having declared his own commission, without which it would have had no object.

outliers.claim: Holds that promises and threatenings addressed to particular men are always conditional, God having made them depend on behaviour, so the Ninevites rightly read a condition that was never stated.
Rejects as over-refined the notion that the city was called great to God because it was the object of his particular care, taking the phrase for the ordinary Hebrew idiom of excellence.

themes: So the people of Nineveh believed God, and proclaimed a fast, and put on sackcloth, from the greatest of them even to the least of them.

6.pericope_label: For word came unto the king of Nineveh, and he arose from his throne, and he laid his robe from him, and covered him with sackcloth, and sat in ashes. And he caused it to be proclaimed and published through Nineveh by the decree of the king and his nobles, saying, Let neither man nor beast, herd nor flock, taste any thing: let them not feed, nor drink water:

schools.summary: Narrate the king's descent from the throne and press the edict's form, technical vocabulary and mourning customs against the Assyrian inscriptions, one of them closing on the impermanence of the change.
Note the speed with which the preaching reached the palace, and argue that the fast issued from the royal edict rather than from popular consent.
Weighs the candidates for the throne and agrees that it was the king's decree that instituted the fast and made it general.

debates.question: Did the fast precede the royal edict or follow from it?

positions.position: The people acted first, on their own spontaneous resolution, and the cry reached the king only afterwards.
The edict came first: the earlier verse is a summary and this one the fuller explanation, since a fast in the royal city by mere popular consent is improbable.
Not Sardanapalus, that dissolute prince, but Pul, who came against Menahem.
More probably a king of Assyria contemporary with Joash, though Pul and Sardanapalus are both proposed.

outliers.claim: Closes on the verdict that however deep the mourning and sincere the repentance of a people obeying their king's command, this repentance was not a lasting one.

Holds that the sackcloth on the animals rests on a true instinct of sympathy between men and the beasts that serve them, which superstition here exaggerated into a hope that their sufferings would appease God's wrath.

themes: For word came unto the king of Nineveh, and he arose from his throne, and he laid his robe from him, and covered him with sackcloth, and sat in ashes.

And he caused it to be proclaimed and published through Nineveh by the decree of the king and his nobles, saying, Let neither man nor beast, herd nor flock, taste any thing: let them not feed, nor drink water:

8.pericope_label: But let man and beast be covered with sackcloth, and cry mightily unto God: yea, let them turn every one from his evil way, and from the violence that is in their hands. Who can tell if God will turn and repent, and turn away from his fierce anger, that we perish not? And God saw their works, that they turned from their evil way; and God repented of the evil, that he had said that he would do unto them; and he did it not.

schools.summary: Presses the demand for a moral change and the charge of violence against what the inscriptions show of Assyrian manners, then confesses ignorance of the manner in which the ruin was averted.
Restrict the works God saw to the inward turning from the evil way, and guard the pardon as freely given rather than procured by the repentance that preceded it.
Illustrates the mourning from classical poetry and reads the outcome as proof that the threatening had been conditional throughout.

debates.question: In what sense did the works God saw bring about the deliverance?

positions.position: Not the outward rites but the inward works, faith and repentance with their fruits, seen so as to be approved and accepted.
The turning from the evil way, a real renovation; but it is not the procuring cause, for God was freely pacified and no satisfaction compensated for former sins.
They returned, the stated condition was met, and so the purpose was changed and the city saved.

outliers.claim: Confesses ignorance both of the nature of the threatened destruction and of the mode in which it was averted, and hopes that some inscription may yet throw light on the question.
Argues that a measure of doubt can coexist with faith, so that the king's who can tell is not despair but a mind still hindered by the sentence pronounced and by conscience of its own guilt.

themes: But let man and beast be covered with sackcloth, and cry mightily unto God: yea, let them turn every one from his evil way, and from the violence that is in their hands.
Who can tell if God will turn and repent, and turn away from his fierce anger, that we perish not?
And God saw their works, that they turned from their evil way; and God repented of the evil, that he had said that he would do unto them; and he did it not.
